1.text:
Why Is Earth the Only World With Moving Plates?

Welcome to the second quarter, where we turn our telescopes around and point them at our own planet. Last quarter you learned that a world's size controls how long it stays hot inside. Now we're going inside Earth itself: its layers, the heat that drives it, the giant plates that drift across its surface, and the earthquakes and volcanoes those plates make.

Here's the big mystery for this deck. Venus, Mars, the Moon and Io all have rocky surfaces, and some even have volcanoes. But as far as we know, Earth is the only world with moving plates. Why us?

We'll finish close to home, with Indiana's own earthquake zones. Yes, Indiana has earthquakes!

Did you know? Indiana has had 71 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or larger since 1812.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

I can describe Earth's layers by what they're made of and how they behave. I can use S-wave shadow zones as evidence for a liquid outer core. I can explain how radioactive decay and leftover heat from Earth's formation drive mantle convection. I can build a timeline from continental drift to plate tectonics. I can model plate boundaries, mountain building and volcano types. I can explain how plates make earthquakes and tsunamis, and rate Indiana's risk.

Two more are enrichment goals that are part of this course. I can use magnitude, knowing each step is about 32 times more energy. And I can compare Earth with Venus, Mars, the Moon and Io to explain why only Earth has plates.

3.text:
Earth's Layers, Two Ways

You can slice Earth into layers two different ways, like sorting a class by height or by birthday. The first way is by what it's made of. The crust and mantle are rock, and the core is iron-nickel metal, split into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Follow the depth scale: the mantle reaches down to about 2,900 km, and the center is 6,371 km down.

The second way is by how the layers behave. The lithosphere is the rigid crust plus the top of the mantle, broken into plates. Below it is the asthenosphere ("astheno" on the slide), hot rock soft enough to flow over long stretches of time, and the plates ride on it. The rest of the mantle is solid but flows slowly. Then the outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid.

The crust is thin, about 5 km under the oceans and about 30 km under continents, up to about 70 km under big mountains. The diagram isn't to scale, so the crust looks much thicker than it really is.

Did you know? The mantle isn't a sea of lava. It's solid rock that creeps very slowly, a little like a glacier. And the inner core is the hottest part, yet it's solid, because the crushing pressure keeps it that way.

4.text:
Seismic Clues

Nobody has ever drilled deeper than about 12 km into Earth, and the center is 6,371 km down. So how do we know what's inside? We listen to earthquakes. Their waves travel through the whole planet, and the way they bend and stop gives away what's down there.

There are two main kinds of waves that travel through the inside of Earth. P waves can travel through solids and liquids. S waves can travel only through solids. When a big earthquake happens, S waves head out in all directions. But on the far side of the planet, beyond about 103° from the quake, no direct S waves arrive.

That gap is the S-wave shadow zone: where no direct S waves arrive, because the liquid outer core stops them. It's the big clue that the outer core is liquid. The core itself was discovered in 1906 from earthquake records.

Did you know? P waves leave a shadow zone too. They get bent at the edge of the core and don't arrive between about 103° and 140° from the quake.

5.text:
Heat Flowing Out of Earth

Earth is constantly leaking heat through its surface, about 47 terawatts (TW) of it. One terawatt is a trillion watts, so that's enough to power about 470 billion 100-watt light bulbs at once.

Where does all that heat come from? Two places. About half of the heat comes from radioactive decay of uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40, atoms spread through Earth's rock. The small numbers are mass numbers. The rest is primordial heat left from formation, when Earth was built from crashing pieces. It still hasn't run out.

Scientists measured the decay part in a sneaky way: they caught tiny particles called geoneutrinos that radioactive decay sends flying out of Earth. This inner heat is what drives everything else in this deck.

Did you know? Earth's inside isn't hot because of the Sun. Sunlight warms only the surface.

6.text:
Mantle Convection

Mantle convection is hot, solid mantle rock slowly rising while cooler rock sinks. Rock heated from below by the core gets less dense and rises. Near the top it cools, gets denser, and sinks again. These loops are called convection cells, and they work like a pot of thick soup on a stove, but millions of times slower.

Two forces at the edges of plates help move them. Ridge push happens at a mid-ocean ridge, where new magma pushes the plates apart. Slab pull happens where a cold, dense plate sinks into the mantle and drags the rest of the plate along behind it.

Which matters more? Most scientists now think slab pull is the main driving force. And remember, the plates ride on the asthenosphere in the upper mantle, not on the liquid core.

7.text:
Why Only Earth Has Plates

Here's the answer to our opening mystery, or at least the best answer so far. Most rocky worlds have a stagnant lid: one unbroken rigid shell, with no moving plates. Earth's lid is different: it's weak enough to break into moving plates that can sink back into the mantle. Why Earth's lid is so weak is still being researched.

Compare the neighbors. Venus has no plates, even though it's about Earth's size and has volcanoes. It's hot and dry, and dry rock may be too stiff to break. Mars has no moving plates, so its volcanoes sit over the same magma source and grow huge, like Olympus Mons. The Moon cooled fast because it's small, and most of its volcanism ended about 3 billion years ago, with small eruptions until about 1 to 2 billion years ago.

Then there's Io, Jupiter's moon. It has no plates, but it's the most volcanic world in the solar system. Its heat comes from tidal heating, as Jupiter and the other moons squeeze and stretch it.

Did you know? Having volcanoes doesn't mean having plates. Venus, Mars and Io all have volcanoes, but none has plate tectonics.

8.text:
Model It: Inside Earth

Time to build two models. For Model A, draw an Earth cutaway with the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. For each layer, label one physical property (solid or liquid? hot? dense?) and one chemical property (made of rock or iron-nickel?).

For Model B, draw convection and plates. Show convection cells with arrows, label the heat sources (decay plus primordial heat), and add ridge push and slab pull.

When you're done, both models together should show what each layer is like and what moves the plates. Double-check yourself: a molten mantle, plates floating on the core, or "the Sun" as a heat source are all signs to look back at Slides 3, 5 and 6.

9.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Let's test your seismic detective skills. Why do S waves never arrive beyond about 103° from a quake?

Is it A) the outer core is liquid, B) the inner core is solid, C) the crust is too thin, or D) the mantle is molten? Think about what S waves can and can't travel through. Pick one and explain why the other three don't work.

10.text:
A Puzzle That Fits

Look at a world map and you might notice something odd: South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces. In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener took that seriously. His idea, continental drift, said the continents move. About 200 million years ago, he argued, they were joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea, which then split apart.

The coastlines fit was only part of his evidence. Fossils of the same plant, Glossopteris, show up on continents now separated by oceans. Glossopteris was a land plant, so it couldn't have swum across. Wegener also found matching rocks on both coasts and old glacier deposits in now-hot Africa.

So did everyone believe him? Not even close. Most scientists rejected the idea, because Wegener couldn't explain what force could move whole continents. That answer took about 50 more years.

11.text:
Stripes on the Seafloor

In the 1950s, ships mapping the ocean floor found two surprises. First, an underwater mountain range runs down the middle of the oceans: the mid-ocean ridge. Second, the rock on the seafloor has a striped "zebra" pattern of magnetism, with stripes of normal and reversed polarity lined up in mirror-image rows on both sides of the ridge.

Scientists already knew that Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times, with north and south trading places. In 1962, Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading: new ocean floor forms at a ridge and moves away on both sides. Magma rises at the ridge, cools into new crust, and slides away like two conveyor belts.

Here's how that makes stripes. As new rock cools, it records the direction of Earth's magnetic field, a bit like a snapshot. Then it's carried away from the ridge. The youngest rock sits at the ridge, and rock gets older as you move away on either side.

Did you know? New crust doesn't make Earth bigger. Old crust sinks back down at deep ocean trenches about as fast as new crust forms.

12.text:
How Old Is the Seafloor?

You might guess the deep ocean floor is the oldest part of Earth. It's actually the youngest! Almost all ocean floor is less than 200 million years old. At the ridge, it's 0 years old, forming right now.

Why so young? The oldest floor sinks back into the mantle at trenches, so it gets recycled. The oldest Pacific floor, near the Marianas, is about 180 million years old. Compare that with Earth itself, at 4.54 billion years. The ocean floor is less than about 4% of Earth's age.

Continents are a different story. Continental rock is too light to sink, so it can hang around for billions of years.

13.text:
Timeline: How the Theory Grew

Big scientific ideas usually aren't one "aha" moment. They grow piece by piece, each step answering the question the last one left open. Here's how plate tectonics grew.

1912: Wegener proposes continental drift. 1950s: ocean surveys find the ridge and magnetic stripes. 1962: Hess proposes seafloor spreading. 1963: Vine and Matthews explain the stripes. 1968: drill cores show that rock ages grow older moving away from the ridge.

Your task: sketch the evidence above each date. Then explain how each step built on the last.

14.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Here's a question about those zebra stripes. Why are the magnetic stripes mirror images across a ridge?

Is it A) new rock forms at the ridge and moves off both ways, B) ships magnetized the rock, C) continents dragged the seafloor, or D) the field flips on one side only? Look back at the conveyor belt on Slide 11. Choose your answer and explain it.

15.text:
Three Kinds of Boundary

A plate boundary is where two plates meet: they pull apart, collide, or slide past. Each kind builds its own landforms.

At a divergent boundary, plates pull apart and new crust forms. That makes ridges and rift valleys, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At a convergent boundary, plates push together. One plate often sinks under the other, building trenches, volcanoes and mountains, like the Andes in South America. At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other, making long faults, like California's San Andreas, about 1,300 km long.

Don't picture plates crashing like bumper cars. They move only a few centimeters per year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Earthquakes happen at all three kinds of boundary, but volcanoes mostly form where plates pull apart or come together.

Did you know? Most plate boundaries aren't on land at all. They're hidden under the oceans.

16.text:
When Plates Collide

Orogeny is mountain building where plates converge. What you get depends on which kinds of plates meet.

When ocean meets continent, the denser ocean plate sinks under the continent, and volcanoes rise along the edge, like the Andes. When ocean meets ocean, one plate sinks under the other, making a deep trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands called an island arc, like the Aleutians off Alaska.

When continent meets continent, neither one sinks, because continental rock is too light. Instead the crust crumples upward like a rug pushed against a wall. That's how India crashing into Asia raised the Himalayas, topped by Everest at 8,849 m, along with the high Tibetan Plateau.

Did you know? Not all mountains are volcanoes. The Himalayas are folded crust, with no volcanoes at all.

17.text:
Where the Biggest Quakes Hit

Earthquakes don't happen just anywhere. 81% of the largest earthquakes strike around the rim of the Pacific Plate, in a belt called the Ring of Fire. That's where plates sink in subduction zones, and it's also home to many active volcanoes.

A second belt runs from the Mediterranean through the Himalayas and has about 17% of the largest quakes, including the huge 2004 earthquake and tsunami in Indonesia. A third belt follows the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

The pattern is the point: earthquakes and volcanoes trace the edges of plates. But quakes can happen inside plates too, and you'll see that right here in Indiana.

18.text:
Hotspots: Hawaii vs. Mars

Most volcanoes sit on plate boundaries. But Hawaii is more than 3,200 km from the nearest one! The explanation is a hotspot: a long-lasting hot region in the mantle that feeds volcanoes far from plate edges.

On Earth, the plate moves over the hotspot, which stays nearly still. Each volcano gets carried away and dies, and a new one grows in its place. So the islands form a chain that gets older to the northwest. The Big Island's rocks are less than 0.7 million years old, while Kauai's are about 5.1 million years old.

Now look at Mars. It has no moving plate, so a volcano stays parked over its magma source and keeps growing. That's how Olympus Mons reached about 22 km tall, compared with Everest at 8,849 m. Both Hawaii's volcanoes and Olympus Mons are shield volcanoes, built from runny lava.

Did you know? Think of a hotspot like a candle under a moving sheet of paper. Slide the paper and you get a line of scorch marks instead of one big hole.

19.text:
3 Ways to Melt a Rock

Almost all of Earth's mantle is solid. So where does the melted rock for volcanoes come from? There are only three ways to melt a rock.

You can heat it, but that's rare. You can drop the pressure: when hot rock rises, the squeeze on it eases, and it can melt. That's what happens at ridges and hotspots. Or you can add water, which lowers the temperature rock needs to melt. That's what happens at subduction zones, where water from the sinking plate seeps into the hot rock above it.

Did you know? At subduction zones, the melting happens about 100 km down, which is why the volcanoes sit back from the trench instead of right at it.

20.text:
Sticky + Gassy = Boom

Why do some volcanoes ooze while others explode? The answer is in the magma. As magma rises, gas dissolved in it expands into bubbles, just like a shaken soda.

The key word is viscosity: resistance to flow. Runny magma lets gas escape easily, so you get gentle flows of lava, like Hawaii's. Sticky, gassy magma traps the bubbles, pressure builds, and it explodes.

What makes magma sticky? Lots of silica. Silica-rich magma is cooler and thicker, so it holds in gas. When it finally blows, the bubbles shatter the magma into volcanic ash, which is really tiny bits of volcanic glass.

21.text:
Model It: Mountains & Volcanoes

Time to build two more models. For Model A, draw orogeny: ocean meets continent, ocean meets ocean, and continent meets continent. For Model B, draw three kinds of volcanoes.

A shield volcano is built from fluid basalt lava, so it's broad and gentle. A composite volcano is built from layers of lava and ash, so it's tall and steep. A cinder cone erupts from one vent, piling up cinders into a small, steep hill.

Draw and label each model. Add where it forms and how its magma makes it look that way.

22.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Think back to the collisions on Slide 16. Which boundary builds a volcanic island arc like the Aleutians?

Is it A) two ocean plates converge, B) two continents collide, C) plates slide past each other, or D) plates pull apart at a ridge? Choose your answer and describe what happens to each plate.

23.text:
Reading a Seismogram

A seismometer records ground shaking over time, and the zigzag line it draws is a seismogram. Read it from left to right. The P wave arrives first, because it's the fastest. The S wave comes next. Then come the surface waves, which bring the strongest shaking.

The gap between the P and S arrivals grows with distance from the quake. Compare that gap at several stations, and you can pinpoint where the quake happened.

Magnitude is a number for an earthquake's energy: +1 means about 32× more. So a magnitude 6 releases about 32 times the energy of a magnitude 5, and about 1,000 times (32 × 32) the energy of a magnitude 4. That's why a small change in the number is a big deal.

Did you know? Magnitude and intensity aren't the same. Magnitude is the size of the quake at its source. Intensity is how hard the ground shakes where you are.

24.text:
Indiana Quakes M3+ Since 1812

Indiana is far from any plate boundary, yet it has had 71 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or larger since 1812. Most happen in southwestern Indiana, in the Wabash Valley Seismic Zone along the Illinois-Indiana line. Old, deeply buried faults there slip from time to time.

The biggest Wabash Valley quake on record was an M5.4 in 1968. More recently, an M5.2 struck near Mt. Carmel, Illinois, early one morning in 2008. It was felt from Wisconsin to Georgia. Moderately damaging quakes happen there every 10 to 20 years.

Just to the southwest is the New Madrid Seismic Zone, which produced the famous 1811 to 1812 sequence, with three main shocks of around magnitude 7. These are intraplate zones: inside a plate, not at its edge.

Did you know? Midwest earthquakes can be felt over an area up to 10 times larger than similar West Coast quakes, because the old, cool, dense bedrock here carries waves farther.

25.text:
How Close Are We to a Fault?

Here's your chance to study your own backyard. Start with a model of how plates slip, cause a quake, and sometimes cause a tsunami. Step 1: a fault locks, then slips. Step 2: waves spread out. Step 3: if the slip happens under the ocean, the seafloor lifts the water, sending out a tsunami.

Then use indianamap.org to fill in the table, and caption each step of your model. For each fault or zone, decide whether it's at a plate edge or intraplate, find its distance from school in km, and look up the liquefaction potential. That's when shaking makes loose, wet ground act like a liquid.

Your table covers the Wabash Valley Seismic Zone, the New Madrid Seismic Zone, the nearest mapped fault, and the San Andreas Fault. Your answers will depend on where your school is.

26.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Time to compare Indiana with California. How is the Wabash Valley zone different from the San Andreas?

Is it A) it is inside a plate, on old buried faults, B) it is a transform plate boundary, C) Indiana sits on a subduction zone, or D) it cannot make earthquakes? Look back at Slides 15 and 24 before you decide. Explain your choice.

27.text:
Exit Ticket

You went from the center of the Earth up to the faults under Indiana. Show what you know with three questions.

First, name one piece of seismic evidence that the outer core is liquid. Second, how did drift, seafloor spreading and magnetic stripes build plate tectonics? Third, why does Earth have moving plates but Venus and Mars do not?

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself again.

29.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.6.1: draw a model of Earth's crust, mantle, outer core and inner core, with their physical and chemical properties. ES.6.3: show how the mantle convects and moves the plates, powered by radioactive decay and leftover heat from Earth's formation, along with ridge push and slab pull. ES.6.4: make a timeline of how plate tectonics developed, showing how continental drift, seafloor spreading and paleomagnetism built on each other.

ES.6.5: model the different kinds of mountain building, and show how ocean and continental plates create features like island arcs and high plateaus. ES.6.6: model and compare shield, composite and cinder cone volcanoes, and explain how lava makeup and location shape them. ES.6.7: explain how plate motion makes earthquakes and tsunamis, use indianamap.org to check how close your school is to faults and liquefaction risk, and tell the difference between faults inside plates, like the Wabash Valley Fault System, and faults at plate edges.
